tip: 'Akad nikah' = the short vow ceremony; the 'resepsi' is the big party afterwards.
'Batik' is wedding wear: a good batik shirt is normally right at a 'resepsi'.
'Calon' = future or -to-be: 'calon mertua' = future in-laws, 'calon suami' = husband-to-be.
Wedding guests give cash in an 'amplop' (envelope), dropped in a box at the door – not handed over.
'Selamat menempuh hidup baru' = the set wedding wish: 'safe journey into the new life'.
'Mertua' = your spouse's parents, 'menantu' = your child's spouse; 'rumah mertua' = the in-laws' house.
'Yang ke-' + number = 'the Nth': 'ulang tahun yang keenam puluh' = the sixtieth birthday.
'Selamat' + noun makes a wish: 'selamat ulang tahun' = happy birthday, 'selamat jalan' = safe travels.
'Kado' = a wrapped present (from Dutch 'cadeau'); 'hadiah' is the wider word for gift or prize.
Indonesian birthdays flip the treat: the birthday person 'mentraktir' (treats) the friends.
'Lebaran' = the Eid homecoming holiday, when much of the country travels to family.
'Mudik' = the big trip home to your family town before 'Lebaran' – millions travel at once.
'Mengobrol' = to chat; in casual speech it is usually shortened to 'ngobrol'.
Adding '-kan' means doing it for someone: 'membuat teh' = made tea, 'membuatkan kami teh' = made tea for us. The person served comes right after the verb.
'Cium tangan' (a child presses the elder's hand to the face) is the usual greeting for grandparents.
'Selamat atas' + noun congratulates: 'selamat atas kelahiran' = congrats on the birth.
'Semoga' + clause = hopefully or may: 'semoga usaha baru kamu berjalan lancar' = may your new business go smoothly.
The Eid greeting: 'mohon maaf lahir dan batin' = forgive my wrongs, outward and inward.
'Selamat' + verb blesses an activity: 'selamat menikmati' = enjoy, 'selamat belajar' = happy studying.
'Kabar' is the noun 'news'; the '-i' ending turns it into a verb: 'kabari kami' = send us word. Indonesian often builds verbs straight from nouns this way.
'Turut berduka cita' = the set condolence, 'I share the grief'; the usual reply is a quiet 'terima kasih'.
'Oleh-oleh' = treats you bring people after a trip – coming home empty-handed is frowned on.
'Titip' = ask a traveler to get you something: 'titip oleh-oleh dodol' = bring me back some dodol.
Object + 'sudah saya' + bare verb = the everyday 'done by me' pattern: 'sudah saya bungkus' = I have wrapped it.
'Membawakan' puts the person right after the verb: 'membawakan keponakan mainan' = brought the nieces and nephews toys.
'Para' + person noun = plural group: 'para tamu' = the guests, 'para sepupu' = the cousins.
'Masing-masing' sits after the noun and covers 'their own' by itself: 'kota masing-masing' = their own cities – no separate word for 'their' needed.
'Bisa' = ability: 'bisa berenang' = can swim. For permission Indonesian normally uses 'boleh', not 'bisa'.
'Bisa' = able (skill), 'boleh' = allowed (permission): 'bisa menyetir, tapi belum boleh'.
'Boleh saya...?' = May I...? – the everyday way to ask permission: 'boleh saya pinjam...?'
